newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Threatened Afghan chief declares valley emergency.
newsitem.headline: Threatened Afghan chief declares valley emergency.

text.p: The military chief of Afghanistan's ousted government has declared a state of emergency in his Panjsher Valley stronghold and ordered an evacuation in anticipation of an attack, his fighters said on Wednesday.

Hundreds of women, children and the elderly clambered out of the valley on a steep, rocky path up the side of a gorge to head for safety into territory controlled by the Islamic Taleban militia that drove Ahmad Shah Masood from Kabul last week.
The only people going in were men of fighting age who said they were returning to defend the Panjsher after taking their families to safety.

The mostly ethnic Pashtun Taleban, who have taken control of three-quarters of Afghanistan since their movement was born in refugee camps in Pakistan two years ago, have said they will attack the Panjsher if Masood does not surrender.

Abdur Razzaq, commander of the Taleban forces which swept north from Kabul over the past few days and bottled up the Panjsher, said on Tuesday a letter had been sent to Masood demanding he surrender or face attack.
His men said they had been ordered to begin the assault early on Wednesday, but there was no sign of fighting and Razzaq refused to say when it might begin.
"Nothing's going on," was all he would say.
But there was no sign among Masood's mostly ethnic Tajik men in the Panjsher that surrender was under consideration. All the activity was aimed at preparing defences.

As refugees trooped out of the valley, an explosion sent up an enormous cloud of dust -- Masood's men had planted more dynamite in the sides of the gorge to bring another landslide down across the narrow road that runs up it alongside a fast-flowing river.
Masood himself watched the blast and took a look at the results, then ordered more, his fighters said.
"He ordered us to seal the valley completly against the Taleban," said one.
If the Taleban do attack the Panjsher, they would enter with enormous difficulty.
Masood's defence of the valley against repeated Soviet assaults in the 1980s won him the reputation of one of the best guerrilla chiefs in the war against the then Moscow-backed communist government.
The Soviet army entered the valley in waves of helicopter landings and still could not hold it. The Taleban have helicopters, but are not known to have used them in warfare.

They would either have to fight their way up the gorge, little more than 50 yards (metres) wide in its early stages with mountain sides rising almost vertically, or come down over the jagged mountain tops.

The track the refugees were using would be equally difficult and was well defended. Masood's fighters guarding it were alert and edgy and said the valley was well stocked with fuel, weapons and ammunition and ready for a long siege once civilians had left.

Women clad in the all-enveloping burqa, which the Taleban have decreed all women should wear in public, led children on the path along the gorge. Many of the smaller children wept as they were carried along the steep trail, a tough hour-long slog for their menfolk.
Most refugees took with them only what they could carry, although one family was driving along a small herd of sheep and goats.
The women carried at most a shopping bag. The few men among them carried large bundles and sweated heavily in the fierce sun.
The men seemed mostly to leave the women and children at the village of Golbahar at the mouth of the gorge to continue their journeys to Tajik relatives outside the valley.
Then they turned back over the rocky track to join the defence of the Panjsher.

The Taleban militia shocked the world when they captured the capital of Kabul on September 27 and executed a former president before banning women from workplaces and imposing other Islamic strictures on society.
